ballTurfSliding.source: Value: Stan Hall, 'When a Mallet Strikes a Ball', section 'Coefficients of Friction' (1994; Oxford Croquet, updated 28 April 2026), https://oxfordcroquet.org/tech/hall/. Upper bound: Don Gugan, 'The Physics of Croquet Strokes: Analysis of the CA high-speed DVD', section 10.2 (2009; Oxford Croquet), https://oxfordcroquet.org/tech/gugan4/
ballTurfSliding.note: Hall measured croquet balls sliding on a croquet court: "The coefficient of sliding friction was measured directly. Three balls were embedded in a sheet of polystyrene, which was then pulled along ... For a fairly fast court (normal, cut to 6mm) the coefficient was 0.48. For a fairly heavy court, the coefficient was 0.53." (Hall also gives rolling friction ≈ 0.065 on a normal court.) Don Gugan, 'Experiments on the Game of Croquet; Bouncing and Rolling Balls', appendix A4 (https://oxfordcroquet.org/tech/gugan1/), adopts Hall's µs = 0.48. Gugan's DVD analysis estimates µs ≈ 1.0 for a ball pressed into the turf in a roll stroke ("double the value of 0.5 obtained under very different conditions by Hall"), which sets the upper bound. The fast-court figure is used because a typical lawn is around 10 s (lawn.json). Since P2b.2b.2b.2a Gugan's impulsive µ ≈ 1.0 (Gugan 4 Table 4(b)) is a held-out check, not an input: it attributes all the ball's horizontal slowing in its pit to friction on flat ground, and the bed's ramp supplies part of it (P2b.2b.2b.2a design §4.3, §4.5).

ballBallRestitution.source: Value: Don Gugan, 'The Physics of Croquet Strokes: Analysis of the CA high-speed DVD', section 4.1 'Clean Scatter Shots' (2009; Oxford Croquet), https://oxfordcroquet.org/tech/gugan4/. Bounds: derived from World Croquet Federation, The Laws of Association Croquet, 7th Edition (February 2021), Appendix 2, A2.1; https://worldcroquet.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/02/Laws-7th-Edition-master-new.pdf
ballBallRestitution.note: Gugan measured ball-on-ball collisions from high-speed video: "The ratio of speeds of the two balls as a result of impact, v2/v1, ... has a mean value of 0.86 ± 0.01 ... This yields e = 0.72 ± 0.02" (v2/v1 = (1 + e)/2), and concludes "Clean scatter shots (section 4) give the CoR, e = 0.72 ± 0.02, near the lower end of the allowable range." Bounds from the drop test (ball.json rebound): e = sqrt(h_rebound / h_drop) = sqrt(30/60) = 0.7071 to sqrt(45/60) = 0.8660. Calladine & Heyman (Engineering, 1962) used e = 3/4 as an illustrative value.

ballBallFriction.source: Value: David Alciatore, 'Illustrated Principles: 90° and 30° Rule Follow-up – Part III: inelasticity and friction', Billiards Digest, April 2005, https://drdavepoolinfo.com/bd_articles/2005/april05.pdf; Rod Cross, 'Billiards' (University of Sydney), https://www.physics.usyd.edu.au/~cross/Billiards.htm. Upper bound: Don Gugan, 'The Physics of Croquet Strokes: Analysis of the CA high-speed DVD', appendix B (2009; Oxford Croquet), https://oxfordcroquet.org/tech/gugan4/
ballBallFriction.note: No croquet ball-on-ball friction measurement was found. Analogue: billiard ball on billiard ball. Alciatore: "Most reported values for pool balls are close to 0.06"; Cross: "The coefficient of sliding friction (COF) between one ball and another is typically only about 0.06." Croquet balls are milled plastic rather than polished phenolic, and croquet players see noticeable 'pull' in split strokes; an Oxford Croquet ball comparison (https://oxfordcroquet.org/tech/invictus/) attributes more pull to deeper milling. The billiard figure is therefore taken as the lower bound. Upper bound: Gugan's generic statement for a croquet ball on a mallet face, "typical values of sliding friction are ≈ 0.5".

ballUprightRestitution.source: Don Gugan, 'Experiments on the Game of Croquet; Bouncing and Rolling Balls', Table I (2002; Oxford Croquet, updated 20 April 2026), https://oxfordcroquet.org/tech/gugan1/; lower bound from World Croquet Federation, The Laws of Association Croquet, 7th Edition (February 2021), Appendix 2, A2.1
ballUprightRestitution.note: Analogue: croquet ball dropped on a rigid steel plate (the CA test surface) standing in for a steel or iron hoop upright. Gugan Table I, Jaques 'Eclipse' ball on steel at 2.83 m/s impact: e = 0.795 (0.848 at 0.5 m/s falling to 0.757 at 6.45 m/s). Bounds: the Laws' minimum ball–steel restitution sqrt(30/60) = 0.7071, and the highest ball-on-steel figure in Table I (Townsend ball, 0.970). An upright is a slender rod set in turf, not a plate set in concrete, so energy lost to hoop movement is not included; Ian Bond, 'Collisions with a Hoop' (https://oxfordcroquet.org/tech/critical/), notes that hoop rigidity and elasticity affect ball–hoop interactions and that hoop materials (aluminium, cast iron, steel) vary.

ballUprightFriction.source: Engineering ToolBox, 'Friction - Coefficients for Common Materials and Surfaces' (2025), https://www.engineeringtoolbox.com/friction-coefficients-d_778.html; Precision Urethane, 'Coefficient of Friction' (static COF against dry steel, ASTM D1894), https://www.precisionurethane.com/coefficient-of-friction.html
ballUprightFriction.note: No croquet ball–hoop friction measurement was found. Modern balls are polyurethane (Dawson patent: "cold cast, entirely from the external surface to the center, of polyurethane plastics material", https://oxfordcroquet.org/tech/dawson/1/). Analogue: rigid plastics on clean dry steel. Engineering ToolBox (static, clean and dry): polyethylene–steel 0.2, polystyrene–steel 0.3–0.35, nylon–steel 0.4, Plexiglas–steel 0.4–0.5. Precision Urethane: hard urethane grades against dry steel 0.11–0.19 (static), softer grades far higher. Value 0.3 sits mid-range; bounds span hard urethane (0.11) to Plexiglas (0.5). Paint on the uprights is not accounted for. Weakly supported.

ballPegRestitution.source: Don Gugan, 'Experiments on the Game of Croquet; Bouncing and Rolling Balls', Table I (2002; Oxford Croquet, updated 20 April 2026), https://oxfordcroquet.org/tech/gugan1/; lower bound from World Croquet Federation, The Laws of Association Croquet, 7th Edition (February 2021), Appendix 2, A2.1
ballPegRestitution.note: Law 5.1.1 requires the peg to be "a rigid cylinder" and "vertical and firmly fixed" but does not specify its material. Analogue: croquet ball dropped on a rigidly clamped wooden mallet head. Gugan Table I, Jaques ball on wood at 2.83 m/s: e = 0.817 (0.857 at 0.5 m/s, 0.795 at 6.01 m/s). Bounds: the Laws' minimum ball–steel restitution 0.7071 and the highest ball-on-wood or ball-on-steel figure in Table I (Townsend ball, 0.970).

ballPegFriction.source: Engineering ToolBox, 'Friction - Coefficients for Common Materials and Surfaces' (2025), https://www.engineeringtoolbox.com/friction-coefficients-d_778.html; Precision Urethane, 'Coefficient of Friction', https://www.precisionurethane.com/coefficient-of-friction.html
ballPegFriction.note: No croquet ball–peg friction measurement was found, and the Laws do not specify the peg's material. Same plastic-ball analogue as ballUprightFriction (value 0.3); the upper bound widens to 0.6 to cover wooden pegs, using Engineering ToolBox wood–clean metal 0.2–0.6 (no plastic–wood figure was found). Weakly supported.

ballTurfRestitution.source: Value and lower bound: Don Gugan, 'The Physics of Croquet Strokes: Analysis of the CA high-speed DVD', section 7.1 (2009; Oxford Croquet), https://oxfordcroquet.org/tech/gugan4/. Upper bound and speed dependence: A. Raymond Penner, 'The run of a golf ball', Can. J. Phys. 80: 931–940 (2002), eq. (5), DOI 10.1139/P02-035, http://raypenner.com/golf-run.pdf
ballTurfRestitution.note: Gugan, from high-speed video of a roll stroke (A4R) in which the ball is driven into the lawn: "the downward velocity of the ball can be estimated to be close to 5 m/s immediately after impact, so comparing this with the upward velocity of 2.48 m/s gives a CoR for the ground of about 0.5. However, courts can be expected to vary greatly depending on their composition, their grass covering, and their dampness, and, for instance, drop tests in Bristol at a speed of about 6 m/s on a typically grassed, 'hard' court resulted in bounce heights of about 50 mm, corresponding to a CoR of only about 0.15." (Check: 6 m/s is a drop of v²/2g = 1.835 m, and sqrt(0.050 / 1.835) = 0.165 ≈ 0.15.) He also notes "The transient hollow formed in the ground is surprisingly large, about 50 mm in diameter". No other croquet ball–lawn restitution figure was found; Gugan, 'Experiments on the Game of Croquet; Bouncing and Rolling Balls' (https://oxfordcroquet.org/tech/gugan1/) tests only steel, wood and plastic. Speed dependence (analogue: golf ball on turf), Penner: "The coefficient of restitution, e, between a golf ball and turf and its dependence on impact speed has previously been measured by Penner [2]. It was found that the value of e decreased with increasing impact speed with the following function providing a good fit to the data: e = 0.510 − 0.0375 |viy| + 0.000903 |viy|², |viy| ⩽ 20 m/s; e = 0.120, |viy| > 20 m/s". At croquet landing speeds this gives 0.47 (1 m/s), 0.44 (2 m/s), 0.35 (5 m/s) and 0.32 (6 m/s). Its low-speed limit, 0.51, sets the upper bound, and the Bristol free drop sets the lower. The value is constant; speed dependence is not modelled.
